findings.title: The truncated-day index cannot see an empty session — the exact shape #22 leaves behind
findings.description:
`build_truncated_day_index` INNER-JOINs `minute_ohlcv` on the session window and requires `max(m.time) <= ts.session_open_utc`; `find_truncated_days` uses the same shape with `bars.newest IS NOT NULL`. A session with **no** bars inside `[session_open_utc, session_close_utc)` therefore produces no row and is never reported as truncated.

That is precisely the #22 shape: `minute_sessions.py`'s own docstring says the 2026-09-10 failure deleted "the row for D's session … with no session bars behind it", and the spillover bar (EODHD's D-1 20:00 ET bar dated D 00:00 UTC) falls *before* session D's open, so it is outside D's window. Consequences:

- `scripts/repair_921_minute_sessions.py#run_verify` computes `residual` from this index, so the `[PASS] truncated symbol-days in the last 5 sessions: 0 (bar: 0)` line is a **false PASS** for empty sessions (only the separate mass bar would still catch them).
- `minute.py#_build_truncated_index` feeds the same index in as `uncovered_days`, so the new trailing seeding cannot re-seed an empty session either — and the coverage index reports day D as covered (the spillover bar is inside day D), so nothing else re-seeds it either.
- `minute.py`'s comment "The repair's index sees exactly those days" (about the 4,278 symbols) is therefore inaccurate, and `minute_sessions.py`'s claim that the daemon and the repair "agree on what a truncated session is" is false for the empty case.

Either widen the truncation signature to include "no bars in the session window" (and make the residual bar count those), or state explicitly that empty sessions are out of the index's scope and add a separate acceptance bar for them.

findings.title: `last_successful_finish` is not normalized against `-infinity`
findings.description:
The new probe reads `stats.last_successful_finish` raw. `src/manta_trading/market/maintenance/cagg_freshness.py` documents this exact hazard: "last_successful_finish is '-infinity' for a policy that has been created but has never completed a run. psycopg cannot load that into a datetime — it raises DataError mid-fetch", and normalizes it with `nullif(s.last_successful_finish, '-infinity'::timestamptz)`.

The new query omits that normalization, so on a policy that has run but never *succeeded*, psycopg raises `DataError` inside `--verify` — an unhandled exception out of `run_verify`, not the intended `[WAIT]`. It also uses an INNER JOIN to `job_stats`, so a policy with no stats row yields `last_refresh = None` → `stale = True` → `[WAIT]` forever with no diagnosis, and the cutover then loops (see the firing finding below). Reuse `cagg_freshness`'s normalization and its `scheduled`/`last_run_status` signals rather than re-reading the catalog with a weaker query.

findings.title: The freshness probe scans raw `minute_ohlcv` with no statement timeout
findings.description: `SELECT max(created_at) FROM minute_ohlcv WHERE time >= %s AND time <= %s` has no symbol predicate, so it must read every row of one session's worth of bars (~2M rows across the universe) and fetch `created_at` from the heap (no index covers it). This is the raw 4.4-billion-row hypertable the repo documents as the §166/§167 latency cliff, and the read carries no `statement_timeout` — unlike its sibling `fetch_session_mass`, which sets `HEALTH_MINUTE_SESSION_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT` and reads the cagg instead. `scripts/repair_921_minute_sessions.py` connects with a bare `psycopg.connect(url)`, so nothing bounds the statement. Add an explicit timeout and a bounded predicate, or derive the freshness from a cagg-side signal.

findings.title: A `[WAIT]` verdict drives further billable firings, with no budget re-check
findings.description:
The firing loop treats "not all bars met" as "fire again":

```python
verify_text = _verify_when_fresh()
if "FAIL" not in verify_text and "[WAIT]" not in verify_text:
    ... break
```

A stale cagg yields `[WAIT]` with no `FAIL`, so the loop **fires again** — up to `MAX_MINUTE_FIRINGS` (6) times. Each trailing firing is ~13,083 × 5 = ~65k credits (the script's own `MIN_CREDITS_TO_START` comment), so a WAIT can spend ~390k credits, and `_refuse_without_budget()` is checked **once**, before the loop. The whole point of #22's cagg gate is that the verdict is *indeterminate*, not that the fix failed; an indeterminate verdict should end (or extend the wait), not buy another firing. Distinguish "the data is not there yet" from "the data is not coming" before spending.

findings.title: Every `[WAIT]` poll re-runs the universe-wide before-image
findings.description: `_verify_when_fresh` polls `--verify` up to `VERIFY_WAIT_POLLS + 1` = 6 times per firing, and `run_verify` ends with `run_check(conn, symbols)`, which walks all ~13k symbols issuing two queries each (`count_row_shapes`, `find_straddling_gap_start`). The repair module's own docstring measures the per-symbol probe at 0.5–0.9 s against production. A single `--verify` is therefore not cheap, and the new poll loop multiplies it by up to 6 per firing (plus a final acceptance call) — the opposite of the bounded-run goal #22 introduced. Split the cheap acceptance measurements from the expensive universe report, or make the poll use a verify mode that only runs the judged-session checks.

findings.title: `MT_RUN = /usr/local/bin/mt-run *` grants root execution of the whole production CLI
findings.description: The header claims the rule is "Exactly the commands those scripts issue, nothing wider", but `mt-run`'s own `run_production_mt` branch execs `/opt/manta-trading/.venv/bin/mt "$@"` as the invoking user (root, under sudo) with every `MT_*` variable sourced from `/etc/manta-trading.env`. `sudo /usr/local/bin/mt-run data migrate apply --track kalshi` is therefore root-equivalent DDL against production. The cutover only needs `mt-run minute` and `mt-run daily`; name those two explicitly (or scope the alias to the pass kinds) instead of `*`.

findings.title: `MT_UNITS = ... systemctl start/stop mt-*` is wider than the stated intent
findings.description: `mt-*` matches every `mt-` unit on the host: `mt-serve.service` (the serving application), `mt-health.service`, `mt-kalshi-pass.service`, and any unit added later. The scripts only issue `stop/start` on `mt-minute-pass.timer` and `mt-daily-pass.timer`, and `stop mt-minute-pass.service`. Listing the four unit names explicitly keeps the rule's blast radius equal to its stated scope.

findings.title: The sudoers rule names a path the code does not compute, and nothing installs the rule
findings.description: `cutover_common.install()` now resolves the installer as `Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "deploy/install-production.sh"` — "Absolute so the sudoers rule … can name it" — but the rule names `/home/manta/source/repos/manta/trading-data/deploy/install-production.sh`. Those coincide only when the script is run from exactly that checkout; from any other clone (or the worktree this slice was reviewed in) `sudo <computed path> …` does not match the rule and sudo denies it, with an opaque error from `install()`. Separately, `deploy/install-production.sh` installs the units, the journald drop-in and `mt-run`, but **not** `deploy/sudoers.d/manta-ops` — the file's install step is a manual comment. Either derive the rule's path from the same source the code uses, or have the installer write it, so the two cannot disagree.

findings.title: The new import blocks are not in isort order
findings.description: The repo's ruff config selects `["E", "F", "W", "I", "UP", "BLE", "ASYNC", "B"]`. The `from cutover_common import (...)` block was sorted before this change (`CutoverError` — a class — first, then the functions alphabetically); the new block is `NOTES_DIR, fire_unit_until, start_log, CutoverError, fire_unit, …`, which is neither constant-then-class-then-function nor alphabetical, so ruff's `I001` fires. The same edit pattern appears in `scripts/repair_921_minute_sessions.py` (`cagg_freshness_for_session` placed before `CheckReport`/`RepairScanTimeout`), and `src/manta_trading/data/acquisition/daemon/minute.py` now lists `data.gaps.repair_921` before `data.gaps.minute_coverage`. Sort the names per ruff's `order-by-type` grouping.

findings.title: The cutover's control flow is driven by substrings of printed text
findings.description: `"[WAIT]" in text` and `"FAIL" not in text` are the only signals separating "accept", "fire again", and "give up" — exactly the "NEVER use user-accessible labels as logical structure" pattern the project guidelines forbid, and fragile in both directions (`FAIL` can appear in any printed line; `[WAIT]` is a label the repair script prints, not a contract). The repair script already has an exit-code vocabulary (`EXIT_OK = 0`, `EXIT_REFUSED = 2`); give WAIT its own exit code and branch on the return code, keeping the printed text for humans only. Note this also currently makes "the cagg is stale" indistinguishable from "the scan was refused" (both exit 2).

findings.title: The minute timer's "staggered 30 minutes behind the daily pass" is now false
findings.description: The `Description=` line and the comment above `OnCalendar` both state the minute pass is staggered 30 minutes behind `mt-daily-pass.timer` (00:35/12:35). With the firing moved to 04:05, only the 13:05 firing is 30 minutes behind (12:35); the 04:05 firing is 3 h 30 min behind the daily 00:35. The rationale for the original staggering ("so the two passes never start simultaneously … both compete for the same provider quota bucket") still applies to 13:05 but the comment now describes a schedule that no longer exists. `deploy/systemd/mt-kalshi-pass.timer` was updated consistently for this change; this one was not.

findings.title: `mt data health` reads the same cagg with no freshness gate, so the two readers can disagree
findings.description: `run_verify`'s docstring says it "reuses the health check's own code path", and it now adds a cagg-freshness gate before `fetch_session_mass`. `health.py#gather` calls `fetch_session_mass` on the same `materialized_only` cagg with no equivalent gate — the module docstring even says the cagg's freshness "is deliberately not re-checked here". After the 04:05 firing the cagg lags the raw bars by up to one refresh interval, so `mt data health` (hourly at :50) can read a session mass that does not yet reflect the pass that just ran, while `--verify` refuses to judge. The new gate belongs in the shared path (`minute_session_mass.py`), not in one caller.

findings.title: The daemon's hot path now depends on the repair module and runs a universe-wide scan every cycle
findings.description: The always-on daemon imports `build_truncated_day_index` and `RepairScanTimeout` from the slice-921 *repair* module and runs an analytical universe scan (`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '600s'`, six-week scan measured at 7.9 s) at the top of every minute cycle. The repair's own module is explicit that "an unmeasured universe must never be reported as a clean one", while here the same scan's timeout degrades to "seed without it" — two opposite policies for the same measurement, now living in two different modules. Consider moving the truncation index into a shared measurement module with one documented policy, and caching it per cycle rather than per phase.

findings.title: A session that the chunk starts inside is never judged
findings.description: `fetch_session_bounds(bounds_conn, symbol, chunk_start, chunk_end)` returns only sessions whose **open** lies in `[chunk_start, chunk_end]`, and `sessions_without_bars` judges only those whose close is `<= chunk_end`. A session that the chunk begins inside (open `< chunk_start`, e.g. a chunk spanning 120 days that starts mid-session) is therefore invisible to the judgement, so the chunk can be declared SUCCESS while that session's early bars are missing. It is not a regression against the old date comparison, but it is a hole in the new predicate's coverage and worth closing deliberately.

findings.title: The first narration line never reaches the cutover log file
findings.description: `say("slice 921 cutover — minute acquisition correctness")` runs before `start_log(...)`, so that line — the one that says which cutover the file belongs to — is printed but not written. `start_log` writes only `cutover log opened <ts>`. Move the `start_log` call above the first `say`, or include the title in the header it writes.
